To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
neural function, injury, stroke subtype, and clinical status predict treatment gains after poststroke rehabilitation.
a multivariate predictive approach incorporating neural function, neural damage, and clinical status is most accurate for predicting treatment gains poststroke.
the combination of neural injury, neural function, and clinical status best predicts treatment gains poststroke.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the best predictors of treatment response to restorative therapies in stroke.
understanding the factors that influence recovery after stroke and the mechanisms by which restorative therapies may improve functional recovery after stroke.
the development of novel therapies for the treatment of stroke.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the combination of pre-stroke neural function, pre-stroke neural injury, and post-stroke clinical status is predictive of the magnitude of motor treatment gains in stroke survivors.
neural function, injury, or stroke type are the most important predictors of treatment gains after stroke, and that the best predictor is a combination of these 3 factors.
the combination of neural function, neural tissue injury, and clinical severity best predicts treatment response in stroke.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
neural function, injury, or both can predict response to treatment, but that a multivariate model is needed to predict the response to a particular treatment.
neural function, injury, as well as clinical status all contribute to the high variability seen in response to restorative therapies post stroke.
the combination of neural injury, function, and clinical status are the best predictors of outcome after stroke.
The main takeaway from our work is that
neural function and injury are both predictive of treatment response, and these 2 variables can be combined to create a predictive model.
a multivariate model including all 3 of these variables (neural function, neural injury and stroke subtype) is the best predictor of response to therapy.
the combination of clinical, neurophysiological, and neuroimaging data provides a better prediction of response to rehabilitation than any one measure alone.
